title: 81% of CLOs Say GenAI Accelerates Legal Work, Can Help Their Teams Demonstrate Value, But Lack the Metrics to Prove it ACC/Everlaw Survey Finds
author: Association of Corporate Counsel · Everlaw

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source reinforces the cluster’s claim that organisational value cannot be inferred from expected efficiency gains or adoption alone. It materially extends the operating-model point with survey evidence that in-house departments rarely track technology ROI or cost-relative outcomes, and identifies reporting infrastructure, data governance and AI-analysis skills as necessary complements. Its benefit claims remain respondent expectations rather than measured outcomes.
qs: Yet if GenAI promises to help teams show their value, most remain under-equipped to prove it: only 12% of in-house teams track technology return on investment, and just 16% track outcomes relative to cost.

st.t: Buyer transformation: Legal departments may capture AI gains
st.an: The survey supports the cluster’s proposition that corporate legal departments expect to capture GenAI-driven efficiency and strategic value, while organisational absorption—especially weak measurement, fragmented data and inadequate infrastructure—limits their ability to prove and realise those gains. Its evidence is primarily reported expectations and current tracking practices, not verified financial returns or completed market-wide transformation.
qs: According to the findings, in-house legal professionals are nearly unanimous in their view that GenAI can help them demonstrate their value to the enterprise—with all but 4% agreeing—while 81% of legal leaders cite greater speed of legal support and matter resolution as top benefits, underscoring how efficiency is driving adoption.
Despite these promises, legal teams cite a lack of infrastructure as the main roadblock to effectively measuring and reporting about their business impact.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s view that expected efficiency gains do not by themselves demonstrate successful legal-workflow transformation. Its survey evidence shows strong buyer-side expectations alongside weak ROI and outcome measurement, fragmented data and limited integration, reinforcing the need for organisational complements, governance, upskilling and systematic evaluation. It does not materially address verification, apprenticeship or lawyer replacement.

kp.k: Survey captures in-house perspectives on GenAI and business value
kp.d: The November 17, 2025 ACC/Everlaw press release reports survey data from 284 chief legal officers, general counsel, and legal operations professionals worldwide. The report is part two of the 2025 GenAI Strategic Value for Corporate Law Departments report; its findings concern respondents’ views and reported measurement practices.
qs: Based on a survey of 284 CLOs, GCs, and legal operations professionals worldwide, The Role of Generative AI in Proving Corporate Law Department Value survey is part two of the 2025 GenAI Strategic Value for Corporate Law Departments report by the ACC in partnership with Everlaw.

kp.k: Respondents see speed and efficiency as leading GenAI benefits
kp.d: The release reports that 81% of legal leaders cite faster legal support and matter resolution as top benefits. Separately, 76% expect GenAI’s greatest impact to be improving internal team efficiency and resourcing. The latter is an expectation about impact, not a measured productivity result.
qs: 81% of legal leaders cite greater speed of legal support and matter resolution as top benefits, underscoring how efficiency is driving adoption.
76% say GenAI’s greatest impact will be improving internal team efficiency and resourcing.

kp.k: Nearly all respondents expect better demonstration of legal value
kp.d: The survey reports that 96% believe GenAI can help demonstrate their legal team’s business value. The release frames this as a shift away from a cost-center identity toward measurable enterprise contribution; ACC president and CEO Jason L. Brown characterizes GenAI as accelerating legal’s evolution into a strategic, data-driven business partner.
qs: A new survey conducted by Everlaw and the Association of Corporate Counsel (ACC) found that a majority (96%) of survey respondents said GenAI technology can help them demonstrate the legal team’s value to the business
This research shows that generative AI is accelerating legal’s evolution from a support function to a strategic, data-driven partner in business decision-making.

kp.k: Outcome measurement lags behind spending measurement
kp.d: Although 83% track outside counsel spend, only 16% track litigation outcomes relative to cost, 12% track technology ROI, 28% track time-to-resolution, 12% track outside counsel performance, and 9% track impact on business outcomes. The release presents this measurement gap as limiting legal departments’ ability to substantiate GenAI’s business value.
qs: While 83% of respondents track outside counsel spend, few are measuring outcomes such as time-to-resolution or legal’s contribution to growth.
Only 16% of legal teams track litigation outcomes relative to cost, and just 12% track technology ROI.
Small minorities also track measures like time-to-resolution (28%), outside counsel performance (12%), or impact on business outcomes (9%).

kp.k: Legal teams anticipate stronger oversight of outside counsel costs
kp.d: Respondents expect GenAI to support buyer-side cost management: 43% believe it will help identify savings on outside counsel services, and 42% expect improved analysis of law firm billing patterns. These are anticipated capabilities rather than reported realized savings.
qs: Legal teams also believe GenAI will help them identify cost saving opportunities on outside counsel services (43%) and improve analysis of law firm billing patterns (42%).

kp.k: Reporting adoption faces fragmented data and limited integration
kp.d: For the next three to five years, 69% rate adopting GenAI for metrics and reporting as critically or very important. More than half identify data fragmentation and limited tool integration as key barriers, and the release describes inadequate infrastructure as the principal obstacle to measuring and reporting business impact.
qs: 69% of respondents say it is “critically” or “very important” to adopt GenAI for metrics and reporting in the next three to five years.
More than half also cite data fragmentation and limited tool integration as key barriers.
Despite these promises, legal teams cite a lack of infrastructure as the main roadblock to effectively measuring and reporting about their business impact.

kp.k: Everlaw recommends reporting investment, security governance, and analytical upskilling
kp.d: Everlaw Strategic Discovery Advisor Chuck Kellner asserts that efficiency gains are real but argues that the next phase requires rigorous proof of results. His recommendations are investment in reporting technology, data-security governance, and targeted training in AI-driven analysis to move from experimentation to systematic performance measurement.
qs: Efficiency wins are real, but the next phase is about proof and capturing results with the same rigor the rest of the enterprise expects

Closing that gap will require strategic investment in reporting technology, strong governance around data security, and targeted upskilling in AI-driven analysis, so legal teams can move from testing GenAI’s potential to systematically measuring performance and demonstrating impact across the business.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: ACC and Everlaw report that legal leaders see GenAI as accelerating legal support, improving internal efficiency, strengthening cost management, and helping departments demonstrate business value.
pts.d: The release reports that 81% cite faster legal support and matter resolution as leading benefits; 76% expect GenAI’s greatest impact to be internal efficiency and resourcing; 43% believe it will help identify savings on outside counsel services; and 42% anticipate better analysis of law-firm billing patterns. It reports that 96% believe GenAI can help demonstrate their department’s enterprise value. ACC president and CEO Jason L. Brown characterizes this as an ongoing shift from a support function to a strategic, data-driven business partner. Everlaw Strategic Discovery Advisor Chuck Kellner asserts that efficiency gains are real but distinguishes them from the next task of systematically proving business impact.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The claims draw on a worldwide survey of 284 corporate legal leaders and operations professionals, supplemented by statements from ACC and Everlaw representatives.
pts.d: The release summarizes part two of the ACC/Everlaw 2025 GenAI Strategic Value for Corporate Law Departments report. Its percentages describe respondents’ views, expectations, and reported measurement practices, rather than quantified productivity gains or measured financial returns. The measurement-gap claim rests on reported tracking rates: outside counsel spend, 83%; time-to-resolution, 28%; litigation outcomes relative to cost, 16%; technology ROI, 12%; outside counsel performance, 12%; and impact on business outcomes, 9%. Brown’s strategic-transformation claim and Kellner’s assertion of real efficiency gains are interpretive statements accompanying the survey. The supplied release does not provide independent performance tests, before-and-after outcome measurements, or detailed sampling methodology.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The November 17, 2025 release describes current perceived benefits and an emerging strategic shift, with a three-to-five-year horizon for prioritizing GenAI-enabled metrics and reporting.
pts.d: Speed benefits and legal’s changing role are framed as already occurring, whereas efficiency, resourcing, and cost-analysis impacts are also expressed as expectations without specific completion dates. The explicit three-to-five-year horizon concerns the importance respondents attach to adoption for metrics and reporting, not a forecast that quantified business value will necessarily be achieved. The release conditions demonstrable impact on overcoming weak measurement infrastructure, fragmented data, and limited integration. Kellner says closing the gap requires investment in reporting technology, data-security governance, and AI-analysis skills.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims primarily concern corporate legal departments and their enterprise stakeholders, with outside counsel affected through prospective client-side cost and billing analysis.
pts.d: CLOs, general counsel, legal operations professionals, and their in-house teams are the central subjects: GenAI is presented as improving their efficiency, resourcing, legal-support speed, reporting, and ability to articulate strategic value. Businesses receiving that legal support are the intended beneficiaries of faster matter resolution and more measurable legal contributions to business decision-making. Outside law firms are implicated through corporate clients’ anticipated identification of savings and analysis of billing patterns; the release does not quantify resulting changes in firm revenues, staffing, or prices. Its business-value claims concern enterprise legal services rather than individual access to justice.
